description: Test your knowledge of PA CV1 | Cardiovascular System.

cards.text: What is arteriosclerosis and what are its three main types?
cards.answer: Arteriosclerosis is thickening and loss of elasticity of arterial walls. The three types are: (1) atherosclerosis (intimal, lipid-driven), (2) arteriolosclerosis (small arteries/arterioles), and (3) Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis (media calcification).

cards.text: Distinguish hyaline arteriolosclerosis from hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis and their clinical associations.
cards.answer: Hyaline: pink, homogeneous thickening from plasma leakage; associated with benign hypertension and diabetes. Hyperplastic (onion-skin lesion): concentric laminated thickening with luminal narrowing; seen in malignant hypertension (diastolic >120 mmHg).

tip.tip: Hyaline = benign HTN/DM; Hyperplastic = malignant HTN with onion rings

cards.text: What is Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis and why does it differ from atherosclerotic plaques?
cards.answer: Dystrophic calcification of the arterial media appearing as ring-like 'pipe-stem' calcifications on X-ray. Does NOT narrow the lumen and is NOT atheromatous, distinguishing it from atherosclerotic stenosis.

tip.tip: Mönckeberg = Media, rings, NO stenosis (just cosmetic calcium)

cards.text: Name the non-modifiable risk factors for atherosclerosis.
cards.answer: Age (risk rises >40 years), male sex (women catch up post-menopause due to oestrogen loss), and genetics/family history (e.g., familial hypercholesterolaemia with LDL-receptor mutations).

tip.tip: ASG: Age, Sex, Genes — you can't change these

cards.text: List the four major modifiable risk factors for atherosclerosis and one mechanism each.
cards.answer: Dyslipidaemia (↑LDL, ↓HDL) — LDL oxidation; hypertension — endothelial injury; smoking — oxidative stress; diabetes mellitus — LDL glycation and endothelial dysfunction.

cards.text: Describe the first step of the response-to-injury hypothesis in atherosclerosis.
cards.answer: Endothelial injury (from turbulence, ox-LDL, hypertension, smoking) causes endothelial dysfunction with loss of protective state and expression of adhesion molecules (VCAM-1, ICAM-1, E-selectin).

tip.tip: Injury breaks the endothelial barrier and turns on adhesion molecules as a 'welcome mat'

cards.text: What happens to LDL in the arterial intima and why is oxidation clinically important?
cards.answer: LDL accumulates in intima and is oxidised by local ROS to ox-LDL. Ox-LDL is proinflammatory and cannot be cleared by normal LDL receptors, driving foam cell formation and plaque progression.

tip.tip: ox-LDL is the 'bad guy' — inflames tissue and clogs the macrophage system

cards.text: Describe the monocyte-to-foam-cell progression in atherosclerotic plaque formation.
cards.answer: Monocytes adhere to activated endothelium (via VCAM-1/MCP-1), migrate into intima, differentiate into macrophages, engulf ox-LDL via scavenger receptors, and become lipid-laden foam cells, the cellular hallmark of early atheromas.

tip.tip: Monocyte → Macrophage → Foam cell (the triad of plaque buildup)
